keyTakeaways: Translation can welcome audiences into a performance without replacing the language, rhythm, and cultural memory that formed it.
A responsible translator needs context, rehearsal time, authority to question the text, and clear credit—not a last-minute approval task.
Per-device language choice can widen the routes into one performance, but phones are not a neutral or universal access answer.
Describe translated surtitles and accessibility captions precisely so audiences know what information and delivery route they will receive.

faq.question: What does translation as hospitality mean in theatre?
faq.answer: It means giving audiences a usable route into a work while allowing its original language and artistic voice to remain alive on stage.

faq.question: Why should a translator be involved beyond final proofreading?
faq.answer: Performance translation needs context, artistic dialogue, rehearsal, authority, and accountability. Those conditions let the translator shape text that belongs to the production.

faq.question: Does mobile language choice work for every audience?
faq.answer: No. It can offer individual language choice, but device access, screen size, attention, venue policy, connectivity, and audience preference must be considered.

faq.question: Are translated surtitles a complete accessibility service?
faq.answer: Not automatically. Accessibility captions may also need speaker information, sound effects, music, and off-stage sound. The production should describe the service precisely.

glossary.definition: Designing translation as an invitation into a work, not as a replacement for its original language.
The rhythm, register, timing, relationships, and cultural memory carried by the language in which a performance was made.
A prepared way for an audience member to follow a performance, such as English surtitles or another reviewed language track.
A delivery model in which audience members select from enabled languages on their own browser-based viewer.
A human operator's work of advancing, holding, hiding, or recovering prepared text in time with a live performance.
